The learned Munsif dismissed the suit after finding that the C.S. record (Ext. 2) indicated that Jasmat Sardar has acquired a tenancy right in the suit land and that there was no evidence that during his life the land was taken back from him and given to some other persons as borga by the plaintiffs predecessors, that the plaintiffs had no possession within 12 years before the date of the institution of the suit. 

 6. Mr. A.T.M. Kamrul Islam, the learned Advocate appearing for the appellant, has submitted that the learned Subordinate Judge misinterpreted the decision in the case of Kumir Mondal Vs. Pramatha Nath Chowdhury (1962) in 14 DL:R 801 in as much as the principle laid down in the said case is that a borgadar recorded in the C.S. Khatian as tenant before the introduction of the proviso to clause (17) of section 3 of the Bengal Tenancy Act, 1885 by the amending Act of 1928 can plead tenancy right even after the introduction of the proviso. He has further submitted that the presumption of correctness of the entry in the C.S. Khatian cannot be held to have been rebutted merely because there is no evidence to show the basis of the entry. Mr. Islam, in support of his contention, has relied on Alimuddin Munshi Vs. Mainuddin Talukdar (1962) 14 DLR 725. 

 7. Mr. B.N. Chowdhury, the learned Advocate for the respondent has submitted that the presumption of the correctness of the record of right has been lost by passage of time, and that where it is on record that Jasmat Sardar  gave kabuliyat to the landlords as a borgadar before the preparation of the C.S. record and there is no other evidence that there had been any other agreement creating a tenancy in favor of Jasmat Sardar  the C.S. record must be held to have been wrongly prepared. 

 8. The case of Kumir Mondal and ors Vs. Pramatha Nath Chowdhury and ors (1962) 14 DLR 801 went up to the Pakistan Supreme Court and the decisionis reported in 17 DLR (SC) at 392. After referring to the history of the legislation of the Bengal Tenancy(Amendment) Act, 1928 and a number of decisions of the Calcutta High Court as well as of the Dacca High Court the Pakistan Supreme Court held: 

 "that this proviso does not debar a person against whom a suit is now filed for recovery of a share of the crop as a bargadar, to set up the defense that he is not a bargadar but a tenant. In such a suit the presumption of correctness of the record of rights may also be invoked in aid as a circumstances supporting the defense but this will certainly not be a conclusive presumption. The presumption that attaches to a record of right under section 103 -B of the Bengal Tenancy Act is only this that the entry in the record of right represents the correct stale of affairs on the elate that it was prepared. Whether that state of affairs is continued even afterwards is not a presumption which arises under this section; but under section 114 of the Evidence Act, and its probative value diminishes progressively with the lapse of time. The older the record the less is its presumptive value. This is a matter therefore, of proof and it merely has the effect of shifting the onus upon the other side. It is certainly not a conclusive proof". 

 11. A finding as to a rebuttal of a statutory presumption is no doubt a finding of fact and it should not ordinarily be disturbed in second appeal. In the present case, however, the finding as to the rebuttal of the presumption of the C,S. record is based on a material mistaken assumption that Jasrnat Sardar would be deemed to have continued in possession as a bargadar on the principle of holding over as enunciated in Section 116 of the Transfer of Property Act and as enunciated in principle under section 51 of the Bengal Tenancy Act. Mr. B.N. Chowdhury has conceded that neither section 166 of the Transfer of Property Act nor section 51 of the Bengal Tenancy Act is applicable to a bargadar. He has, however, contended that the principle of holding over has been applied by way of analogy. The right of holding over, unless conferred by a statute, cannot be implied or inferred by analogy. Long five years after the terms of the borga kabuliyat expired, the C.S. Khatian was published on 6-9-25. The assumption of the Court of appeal below that the settlement operation actually began at the stage when the terms of the borga lease did not expire is based on no evidence. 

 12. Again the learned Subordinate Judge seems to have proceeded on the view that the term 'borgadar' itself is a negation of the right of tenancy. I may refer to the following observation made by D.C. Bhattacharya, J. In Soda Mia Vs. MomrajBhuiya(1974) 26 DLR 245. 

 "It has not been defined anywhere what a 'bargadar is? We find in Wilson's Glossaries, that the term 'barga' has been defined as an agreement by which the cultivator engages to pay the landlord half of the produce, the latter providing half of the seed and paying the whole of the rent, from the definition of 'tenant' as given in section 3, . clause (17) of the Bengal Tenancy Act, as it stood before the amendment of 1929, we find that a tenant means a person who holds land under another person, and is, or but for a special contract would be liable to pay rent for that land to that person, and in clause (13) of the same section 'rent' has been defined as whatever is lawfully payable or deliverable in money or kind by a tenant to his landlord on account of the use or occupation of the land held by the tenant, So we find that there is nothing in clause (13), or clause (17) of section 3 which militates against a bargadar being a tenant, Rent, according to clause (13) of section 3 as we have seen may be in money or in kind and it need not be a fixed amount, there is nothing in law to prevent a landlord from accepting a variable or fluctuating quantity of the produce of land as rent, Therefore, according to the provisions of law, as were in force before 1929, there was nothing inherently inconsistent between the characters of a bargadarand a tenant, " 

 13, In 1929 by an amendment of the Bengal Tenancy Act, the Legislature sought to bring about a certain change with regard to presumption about the status of a person who used to cultivate lands under barga system, by adding the following provision to the definition of 'tenant' to section 3(17) of B,T. Act. 

 “Merely because there is no evidence to show the basis of the entries in the 'record-or-rights, the presumption is not rebutted in view of the provision of section l03(B) of the Bengal Tenancy Act, and also the procedure as laid down in the several sections of the Bengal Tenancy Act followed by the officer concerned while preparing the final records-of-rights. There mutbe further evidence to show that the entries are incorrect. The absence of evidence for the basis of the entries may be a circumstance which along with other evidence may be to show that the presumption has been rebutted. " 

 17. D.W. 1 Osman Ali, stated that Jasmat possessed the land as tenant and after his death his heirs defendants 3,4 and 5 got the suit land ; that he purchased the interest of defendants 3, 4 and 5 by registered kabalas Ext. 1 and l(a); that the suit land was at first recorded in the names of defendants 3, 4 and 5 and the Majumdar landlords filed an objection, under section 19(1) of East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, and got their names recorded but the defendants, 3, 4 and 5 preferred an appeal, under section 19(2) of the said Act, and the land was again in their names. Ext. C is the certified copy of that judgment of the appellate officer. The Government also collected rent from the defendant No. 4 vide Ext. B Defendant's categorical statement that Jasmat got tenancy right in the suit land and after his death his heirs were possessing the same before his purchase are corroborated by D.W. 2 Haji Monsurulla, the tahsildar and D.W. 2 Majan Shah who held land contiguous to the suit land.
